questions.stem: Normal rain has a pH of about 5.5, which is slightly acidic. What makes normal rain acidic even without pollution?

options.text: Nitrogen in the air dissolves in rain
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere dissolves in rainwater to form weak carbonic acid
Oxygen makes water acidic
Water is naturally acidic

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide naturally present in the atmosphere dissolves in rainwater to form carbonic acid: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃. This weak acid gives normal rain a pH of about 5.5. Acid rain (pH below 5) is caused by additional pollutants — mainly sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides — dissolving in rainwater to form stronger acids.

questions.stem: Acid rain damages limestone buildings and marble statues. The limestone (calcium carbonate) fizzes when acid rain falls on it. What reaction is occurring?

options.text: The limestone is melting from the heat of the acid
Calcium carbonate reacts with the acid to produce a soluble salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas (the fizzing)
The limestone is dissolving in pure water
The acid is decomposing into its elements

questions.explanation: Acid rain contains sulfuric and nitric acids that react with calcium carbonate in limestone: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ causes fizzing, and the soluble calcium sulfate washes away, gradually eroding the stone. This is why many historic buildings and statues in polluted areas show significant erosion damage.

questions.stem: Acid rain can fall hundreds of kilometres from where the pollutants were released. A country with very few factories experiences acid rain damage to its forests. How is this possible?

options.text: The forests are producing their own acid
Prevailing winds carry SO₂ and NOₓ from industrialised neighbouring countries, where they form acid rain that falls far from the source
Acid rain can only fall within 1 km of the pollution source
The country must have hidden factories

questions.explanation: SO₂ and NOₓ are gases that can be carried hundreds or even thousands of kilometres by prevailing winds before dissolving in rainwater and falling as acid rain. This is why acid rain is a transboundary pollution problem — Scandinavian countries suffered acid rain damage from UK and European industrial emissions. International agreements have been needed to address this cross-border issue.

questions.stem: When acid rain enters a lake, the pH drops and fish begin to die. A local council adds powdered limestone (calcium carbonate) to the lake. Why does this help?

options.text: Limestone provides food for the fish
Limestone is a base that neutralises the acid, raising the pH back towards neutral
Limestone absorbs water, making the lake shallower
Limestone releases oxygen into the water

questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate (limestone) is a base that reacts with and neutralises acids: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂. Adding it to acidified lakes raises the pH, making the water less acidic and more habitable for fish and other aquatic life. This is called 'liming' and is used as a short-term treatment, but it does not address the root cause of the pollution.

questions.stem: Both sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides contribute to acid rain. Which acids do they form, and how?

options.text: SO₂ forms hydrochloric acid; NOₓ forms carbonic acid
SO₂ forms sulfurous/sulfuric acid; NOₓ forms nitric acid, both by dissolving in rainwater and reacting with water and oxygen
Both form the same acid — nitric acid
They form acids only when mixed together

questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater and is oxidised to form sulfuric acid: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid), and further oxidation gives H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid). Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form nitric acid: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Both are strong acids with pH well below 5, causing the damaging effects of acid rain.
